title: Why Mercurey tastes the way it does

lede.text: Mercurey's vineyards face the rising sun, so they warm early in the morning and sit away from the morning fogs of the plain. Pinot Noir covers 87% of the vines, and the reds are elegant and powerful at once.

chapters.title: Limestone slopes beside the Saône plain
paras: Mercurey belongs to the Côte chalonnaise, about ten kilometres west of Chalon-sur-Saône. This limestone relief runs north to south and faces generally east. It marks the edge between the limestone foothills of the granite Mont-Saint-Vincent massif to the west and the Saône plain to the east.

The vineyards lie on the flanks of two perpendicular valleys that drain the Côte chalonnaise. The topography is complex. Layers of hard limestone alternate with marl, a clayey limestone that resists erosion less. The result is a string of wooded ridges, with marl-soil hollows called combes between them, planted with vines.
The appellation covers just two communes, Mercurey and Saint-Martin-sous-Montaigu. In 2010 it held 677 hectares of vines.

fly.label: Mercurey and its combes
fly.caption: Vines fill the marl hollows between wooded ridges on the Côte chalonnaise.

fly.label: Chalon-sur-Saône and the plain
fly.caption: The Saône plain lies east of the Côte chalonnaise. Chalon-sur-Saône is about ten kilometres east of the vineyards.

chapters.title: Mild, sunny and evenly wet
paras: The climate is a degraded oceanic one, with southern and continental influences. Southern mildness comes up the Saône valley and softens the oceanic influence. It brings very sunny summer months.
Annual rain averages under 800 mm and falls evenly through the year, with no summer drought.
The general exposure of the vineyards lets the air warm quickly early in the morning. Early warmth and shelter from the plain's fogs make conditions that favour great wines.

chapters.title: Stones that drain
paras: The vines grow on slopes between 220 and 350 metres, facing various directions. The soils are mostly limy. On the slopes they mostly form on a thin layer of stony colluvium, debris washed down the hill. The limestone bedrock lies a few decimetres down.
On the western ridges, patches of clay with chailles (flint nodules) make soils that are more acid and very stony, and sometimes very free-draining.
All the soils drain very well. Limestone bedrock and a cover of stones, together with the relief, give optimal drainage that offsets the even rainfall.

chapters.title: Pinot Noir and named plots
paras: Mercurey makes dry still reds and whites. Pinot Noir is the main grape and covers 87% of the vines. Chardonnay and Pinot Gris are the other grapes allowed.
Traditional Burgundian winemaking favours a long life for the reds. Most reds are aged in barrel, especially the premier crus. The whites are dry and generally described as rich and powerful.

Growers often name their wines after the climat, the regional word for a named plot. Some climats, the best exposed and generally on limestone, can carry the mention premier cru. Thirty-two climats are listed, such as Clos des Barraults and Les Byots.

A premier cru climat goes straight after the appellation name, in letters no bigger than it. A cadastral lieu-dit, a registered place name, can also appear if it is on the harvest declaration. Its letters are at most half the size of the appellation name.
Labels may add the wider name Vin de Bourgogne or Grand Vin de Bourgogne. A grape name stays out of the field of the compulsory details, in letters no taller than 2 millimetres.

Mercurey was long sold under the name vin de Beaune. The appellation was recognised by decree in 1936. The first premier cru climats followed in 1943. Growers sell 60% of the wine directly, and merchants remain strong in the trade.
